title: Hash Tables
description: Learn how hash tables map keys to values, handle collisions, and deliver near-constant-time lookups.

data.text: A hash table stores key-value pairs and can usually find a value by its key in near-constant time. The speed comes from a hash function that converts a key into an array index. Understanding how that function works, and what happens when two keys map to the same index, is the key to using hash tables effectively.

The hash function takes a key and returns an integer. The table then uses that integer modulo the table size to pick a bucket. A good hash function distributes keys evenly and is deterministic: the same key always produces the same bucket.

data.title: Simple hash function
data.content: A basic hash function that sums character codes and applies modulo.

data.text: Two different keys can hash to the same bucket. That event is called a collision. Two common strategies for handling collisions are chaining and open addressing.

data.title: Collision strategies
items: Chaining stores a linked list at each bucket. Collisions become extra nodes in that list.
Open addressing searches for the next available slot using probing: linear, quadratic, or double hashing.
Chaining is simpler and degrades gracefully.
Open addressing saves memory but requires careful resizing and load-factor management.

data.text: The load factor is the number of stored items divided by the number of buckets. As the load factor grows, collisions increase and performance drops. Most implementations automatically resize the table and redistribute all keys when the load factor crosses a threshold, typically around 0.75.

data.title: Why resizing is expensive
data.text: Rehashing touches every entry, so a single insertion can take O(n) time. The cost is amortized over many insertions, which is why the average insert remains O(1), but it can cause a noticeable pause for very large tables.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Hash tables trade memory for speed.
A good hash function reduces collisions.
Chaining is the most common collision strategy.
Load factor and resizing affect worst-case latency.
data.takeaway: Hash tables are the go-to structure for key-based lookups, and understanding their internals helps you avoid surprising performance issues.
